content: 1. Shimakawa Y and colleagues conducted a longitudinal population-based study in The Gambia to investigate the natural history of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in West Africa. The study was published in Gut in December 2016 and provides valuable insights into the progression of chronic HBV in this region. 2. Thompson AJV and colleagues explored the relationship between serum hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) titers with disease phase, viral load, and intrahepatic HBV markers. Their findings, published in Hepatology in June 2010, highlight how disease phase influences these correlations. 3. Shimakawa Y and colleagues proposed the use of hepatitis B core-related antigen (HBcrAg) as an alternative to HBV DNA for assessing treatment eligibility in African populations. This study, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, emphasizes the potential of HBcrAg as a cost-effective and accessible marker for treatment decisions. 4. The QUADAS-2 protocol was used to assess the risk of bias in patient selection for studies. It evaluates whether consecutive or random samples of patients were enrolled, whether case-control designs were avoided, and whether inappropriate exclusions were avoided. The applicability of the included patients and settings to the review question was also assessed. 5. The primary objective of the review was to evaluate the performance of HBeAg as an alternative to HBV DNA for determining eligibility for antiviral therapy initiation in pregnant women who are HBsAg-positive. Studies that included only selected pregnant women based on HBV DNA levels or HBeAg serostatus were deemed less relevant to the review question. 6. The risk of bias in the conduct or interpretation of the index test was assessed using signaling questions. These questions evaluated whether the index test results were interpreted without knowledge of the reference standard results and whether any thresholds used were pre-specified. 7. The reference standard's ability to correctly classify the target condition was evaluated. Studies using non-validated in-house methods or failing to describe the reference test were rated as having a higher risk of bias. Blinding of the reference standard results to the index test results was also assessed. 8. The flow and timing of patient testing were evaluated to determine the risk of bias. This included assessing whether the same sample was used for both HBeAg and HBV DNA testing, whether all patients received the same reference standard, and whether all enrolled patients were included in the analysis. 9. Data extraction for the review included publication details, study design, recruitment period, inclusion and exclusion criteria, maternal and infant HBV markers, and preventive measures. Specific details such as the type of assay used, timing of sample collection, and maternal antiviral therapy during pregnancy were recorded. 10. Outcomes of interest included the sensitivity and specificity of HBeAg to diagnose high viremia, the ability of maternal HBeAg during pregnancy to predict mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HBV, and the definition of MTCT based on infant HBsAg or HBV DNA positivity. 11. Preventive measures assessed included maternal antiviral therapy during pregnancy, timely administration of the first dose of the HBV vaccine (within 24 hours of birth), administration of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) at birth, and completion of the three-dose HBV vaccine series. 12. The characteristics of the study population, including maternal age, HBV viral genotypes, and co-infections with HIV, HCV, or HDV, were documented. The outcomes of interest were analyzed based on these characteristics to provide a comprehensive understanding of the factors influencing HBV transmission and treatment outcomes.
